schema: anatomy rows v1 (design.md section 5). shape and label are JSON descriptors: a number set, or {fn: ...} naming the live code value. kinds: surface, band, point, screen. tags: measured (solid), model (dashed), mathematics (dotted, K only).

checkedKey.web: number confirmed on the cited page in this pass
checkedKey.code: computed by or read from the wallpaper's code
checkedKey.secondary: confirmed only through a secondary page or search summary of the cited source
checkedKey.recalled: not confirmed on the web in this pass

bodies.title: Sagittarius A*
bodies.headline: A spinning black hole, seen from the side. The flat edge and the bright side are the same side: the one turning toward you.

rows.name: Shadow
rows.fact: The shadow, 4.77 Rs wide from the side: about Mercury's distance from the Sun.
rows.source: lib/kerr.js at a/M = 0.94 (Background.qml holeSpin); Rs from lib/fall.js (4.15e6 Msun)

rows.name: Flat edge
rows.label: 1.32 Rs
rows.fact: The spin carries light with it, so light can skim closer on this side.
rows.source: lib/kerr.js at a/M = 0.94 (Background.qml holeSpin); Rs from lib/fall.js (4.15e6 Msun)

rows.name: Round edge

shape.fn: shadowOutline: point farthest from the centre

rows.label: 3.45 Rs
rows.fact: On this side light meets the spin head-on, so the shadow reaches wider.
rows.source: lib/kerr.js at a/M = 0.94 (Background.qml holeSpin); Rs from lib/fall.js (4.15e6 Msun)

rows.name: Without spin
rows.label: 5.20 Rs
rows.fact: Without spin the shadow would be this circle.
rows.source: lib/kerr.js at a/M = 0.94 (Background.qml holeSpin); Rs from lib/fall.js (4.15e6 Msun)

rows.name: Centre and offset
rows.label: 1.06 Rs
rows.fact: The hole sits here. Its shadow is pushed to one side by the spin.
rows.source: lib/kerr.js at a/M = 0.94 (Background.qml holeSpin); Rs from lib/fall.js (4.15e6 Msun)

rows.name: Spin axis
rows.label: one turn in 6.1 min
rows.fact: Spin 0.94 is one best-fit model. The horizon turns once in 6.1 minutes, and the depth of the D depends on it.
rows.source: lib/kerr.js at a/M = 0.94 (Background.qml holeSpin); Rs from lib/fall.js (4.15e6 Msun); EHT Collaboration 2022, ApJL 930 L12 (Sgr A* Paper I)

rows.name: Event horizon
rows.label: 0.67 Rs
rows.fact: The event horizon. The shadow around it is about three times wider, because light bends.
rows.source: lib/kerr.js at a/M = 0.94 (Background.qml holeSpin); Rs from lib/fall.js (4.15e6 Msun)

rows.name: Ergosphere
rows.label: 1.0 Rs at the equator
rows.fact: Inside here, space itself is carried round with the hole.
rows.source: lib/kerr.js at a/M = 0.94 (Background.qml holeSpin); Rs from lib/fall.js (4.15e6 Msun)

rows.name: Photon shell
rows.label: 0.71 to 1.97 Rs
rows.fact: Light can circle the hole between these two rings.
rows.source: lib/kerr.js at a/M = 0.94 (Background.qml holeSpin); Rs from lib/fall.js (4.15e6 Msun)

rows.name: Inner edge of the gas
rows.label: 1.01 Rs, 8.2 min orbit
rows.fact: Gas orbits down to here, once every 8.2 minutes.
rows.source: lib/kerr.js at a/M = 0.94 (Background.qml holeSpin); Rs from lib/fall.js (4.15e6 Msun)

rows.name: Bright side
rows.fact: This gas is coming toward you, so its light arrives concentrated and bluer: N times brighter than the far side.
rows.source: lib/kerr.js at a/M = 0.94 (Background.qml holeSpin); Rs from lib/fall.js (4.15e6 Msun)

rows.name: Dim side
rows.fact: This gas is moving away, so its light arrives thinned out and redder.
rows.source: lib/kerr.js at a/M = 0.94 (Background.qml holeSpin); Rs from lib/fall.js (4.15e6 Msun)

rows.name: Measured ring
rows.label: 5.2 Rs across
rows.fact: The Event Horizon Telescope measured a glowing ring this wide in 2017: 51.8 millionths of an arcsecond.
rows.source: EHT Collaboration 2022, ApJL 930 L12 (Sgr A* Paper I)
rows.derived: 51.8 +/- 2.3 microarcsec / (Rs 1.2256e7 km at the code's 8150 pc = 10.05 microarcsec) = 5.15 Rs

rows.name: Inner horizon
rows.label: 0.33 Rs
rows.fact: A second horizon inside the first. The equations go on through it; nature may not.
rows.source: lib/kerr.js at a/M = 0.94 (Background.qml holeSpin); Rs from lib/fall.js (4.15e6 Msun)

rows.name: Ring singularity
rows.label: 0.47 Rs
rows.fact: In a spinning hole the centre is a ring, not a point.
rows.source: lib/kerr.js at a/M = 0.94 (Background.qml holeSpin); Rs from lib/fall.js (4.15e6 Msun)

rows.name: Far sheet
rows.label: through the ring
rows.fact: Through the ring the equations open onto another space. Nothing says it is real.
rows.source: lib/kerr.js at a/M = 0.94 (Background.qml holeSpin); Rs from lib/fall.js (4.15e6 Msun)

rows.name: Star S2's closest pass
rows.label: 120 AU
rows.fact: The star S2 dives to here every 16 years, at 7,650 km a second.
rows.source: GRAVITY Collaboration 2018, A&A 615 L15
rows.derived: 120 AU / Rs(1.2256e7 km) = 1,465 Rs; the paper's rounded figure is ~1,400 Rs

rows.name: Nuclear star cluster
rows.label: 4.2 pc
rows.fact: Half the light of the 25 million Suns crowded round the hole comes from inside here.
rows.source: Schoedel et al. 2014, A&A 566 A47

bodies.title: Sun
bodies.headline: A ball of glowing gas with a furnace at its heart. Its wind blows a bubble that reaches four times farther than Neptune.

rows.name: Core
rows.label: 0.25 R
rows.fact: Almost all the Sun's power is made in this inner quarter, at 15 million degrees.
rows.source: Solar core, Wikipedia (99% of fusion power inside 0.24 R); NASA Science: Sun facts

rows.name: Tachocline
rows.label: 0.713 R
rows.fact: Below this line energy creeps out as light. Above it the gas boils, carrying heat up to the surface.
rows.source: Christensen-Dalsgaard et al. 1991; Basu & Antia 1997 (0.713 R), as reviewed in arXiv:1003.3888

rows.name: Photosphere
rows.label: 695,700 km
rows.fact: The surface we see, 5,500 °C. The thin corona above it reaches 2 million.
rows.source: NASA Sun Fact Sheet (NSSDCA); NASA Science: Sun facts

rows.name: Edge of the corona
rows.label: about 19 R
rows.fact: Inside here the gas still belongs to the Sun. Parker Solar Probe first flew in at 18.8 radii in 2021.
rows.source: NASA SVS 4958, Parker Solar Probe: crossing the Alfven surface (28 Apr 2021, 18.8 Rsun)
rows.note: The Alfven surface is wrinkled and moves; pre-crossing estimates were 10 to 20 Rsun.

rows.name: Termination shock
rows.label: 84 to 94 AU
rows.fact: Here the Sun's wind drops below the speed of sound. The Voyagers crossed at 94 and 84 AU.
rows.source: NASA Voyager interstellar mission

rows.name: Heliopause
rows.label: about 120 AU
rows.fact: The Sun's wind reaches this far. Voyager 1 crossed at 121.6 AU in 2012, Voyager 2 at 119.
rows.source: NASA Voyager interstellar mission; Voyager 2 heliopause papers 2019, Nature Astronomy (summary in Eos)

bodies.title: Mercury
bodies.headline: A small world that is mostly metal: an iron core wrapped in a thin shell of rock.

rows.name: Solid inner core
rows.label: about 1,000 km
rows.fact: A solid iron heart about half the width of the whole core, close to the size of Earth's.
rows.source: Genova et al. 2019, GRL 46, 3625
rows.note: Genova 2019: inner core 0.3 to 0.7 of the outer core radius.

rows.name: Core
rows.label: 2,074 km
rows.fact: Mostly core: iron fills 85% of the radius, and part of it is molten.
rows.source: NASA Science: Mercury facts

rows.name: Surface
rows.label: 2,439.7 km
rows.fact: Rock only about 400 km thick lies over the great core.
rows.source: NASA Mercury Fact Sheet (NSSDCA); NASA Science: Mercury facts

bodies.title: Venus
bodies.headline: Earth's twin in size, wrapped in unbroken cloud over the hottest surface of any planet.

rows.name: Core
rows.label: about 3,200 km
rows.fact: An iron core much like Earth's, sized by models: no seismometer has listened here yet.
rows.source: Venus review 2024 (clouds 47 to 70 km; core 3,200 km model; Margot et al. 2021: 3,500 +/- 500 km)

rows.name: Surface
rows.label: 6,051.8 km
rows.fact: Rock at 464 °C under air 92 times as heavy as ours.
rows.source: NASA Venus Fact Sheet (NSSDCA)

rows.name: Cloud deck
rows.label: 48 to 70 km up
rows.fact: Clouds of sulfuric acid, over 20 km deep, cover the whole planet.
rows.source: Venus review 2024 (clouds 47 to 70 km; core 3,200 km model; Margot et al. 2021: 3,500 +/- 500 km)

bodies.title: Earth
bodies.headline: Iron at the centre, rock around it, a skin of sea and air, and a magnetic shield far out in space.

rows.name: Inner core
rows.label: 1,221 km
rows.fact: Solid iron and nickel, about as hot as the Sun's surface.
rows.source: NASA Science: Earth facts

rows.name: Outer core
rows.label: 2,890 km down
rows.fact: Liquid iron, 2,300 km deep. Its slow churning makes Earth's magnetic field.
rows.source: NASA Science: Earth facts; NASA Earth Fact Sheet (NSSDCA)

rows.name: Mantle
rows.label: 2,900 km thick
rows.fact: Hot rock that flows like thick caramel over millions of years.
rows.source: NASA Science: Earth facts

rows.name: Crust and ocean
rows.label: 30 km on land, 5 at sea
rows.fact: The ground we live on: 30 km thick under land, 5 under the sea floor.
rows.source: NASA Science: Earth facts

rows.name: Inner Van Allen belt
rows.label: 1,600 to 13,000 km up
rows.fact: Fast protons held by Earth's magnetic field.
rows.source: NASA SVS 11212, Van Allen belts

rows.name: Outer Van Allen belt
rows.label: 19,000 to 40,000 km up
rows.fact: A wider ring of fast electrons that swells and shrinks with the Sun's weather.
rows.source: NASA SVS 11212, Van Allen belts

rows.name: Magnetopause
rows.label: about 10 Earth radii
rows.fact: Earth's magnetic shield holds the Sun's wind off here, 10 Earth radii out on the day side.
rows.source: NOAA SWPC: Earth's magnetosphere

bodies.title: Moon
bodies.headline: A small world with a small heart: its iron core fills only a fifth of the radius.

rows.name: Solid inner core
rows.label: 240 km
rows.fact: A solid iron ball, found in 2011 in the Apollo seismometers' old recordings.
rows.source: Weber et al. 2011, Science 331, 309 (NASA release)

rows.name: Fluid outer core
rows.label: 330 km
rows.fact: Liquid iron around the solid heart.
rows.source: Weber et al. 2011, Science 331, 309 (NASA release)

rows.name: Partly molten layer
rows.label: 480 km
rows.fact: Soft, partly melted rock wraps the core.
rows.source: Weber et al. 2011, Science 331, 309 (NASA release)

rows.name: Crust
rows.label: 34 to 43 km thick
rows.fact: The pale crust is 34 to 43 km thick, weighed from orbit by the GRAIL twins.
rows.source: Wieczorek et al. 2013, Science 339, 671; NASA Moon Fact Sheet (NSSDCA)

bodies.title: Mars
bodies.headline: A cold desert with a liquid metal heart, measured by one lander listening for marsquakes.

rows.name: Liquid core
rows.label: 1,650 to 1,830 km
rows.fact: Liquid iron, sized from marsquakes. The newest readings put its edge near 1,650 km.
rows.source: NASA Mars Fact Sheet (NSSDCA), with its 1,650 to 1,675 km footnote

rows.name: Surface
rows.label: 3,389.5 km
rows.fact: Under the red dust the crust is 24 to 72 km thick.
rows.source: NASA Mars Fact Sheet (NSSDCA), with its 1,650 to 1,675 km footnote; Knapmeyer-Endrun et al. 2021, Science 373, 438 (summary)

bodies.title: Jupiter
bodies.headline: A giant with no ground. Clouds give way to an ocean of hydrogen squeezed until it acts like metal.

rows.name: Dilute core
rows.label: to about 0.6 R
rows.fact: No hard centre: heavy elements are mixed through the inner 60% of the radius.
rows.source: Militzer et al. 2022, PSJ 3, 185

rows.name: Metallic hydrogen
rows.label: from about 0.8 R
rows.fact: Below here hydrogen is pressed so hard it carries electricity like a metal, and makes the magnetic field.
rows.source: Planetary models and laboratory work (transition near 0.8 to 0.9 R); NASA Science: Jupiter facts

rows.name: Cloud tops
rows.label: 71,488 by 66,842 km
rows.fact: A day under 10 hours flattens Jupiter: 9,300 km wider than it is tall.
rows.source: Juno radio occultations, Nature Astronomy 2026 (NASA release)
rows.note: Juno 2026 values at the 1-bar level; the NSSDCA fact sheet still lists 71,492 by 66,854 km. The code's mean radius 69,911 km is the older mean (new: 69,886).

rows.name: Io's ring of gas
rows.label: 5.9 Jupiter radii
rows.fact: Volcanoes on the moon Io feed a glowing ring of gas along its orbit.
rows.source: Io orbit 421,700 km = 5.9 RJ (Juno torus occultations)

rows.name: Magnetopause
rows.label: 63 to 92 radii
rows.fact: The largest structure the planets own: its magnetic bubble starts 63 to 92 radii sunward.
rows.source: Joy et al. 2002, JGR 107, 1309
rows.note: NASA's Jupiter page gives 1 to 3 million km (14 to 42 radii), which disagrees with Joy et al. 2002; the paper is used.

bodies.title: Saturn
bodies.headline: The most flattened planet, circled by rings as wide as two thirds of the way from Earth to the Moon.

rows.name: Fuzzy core
rows.label: to about 0.6 R
rows.fact: Ripples in the rings show a core with no edge, spread over 60% of the radius.
rows.source: Mankovich & Fuller 2021, Nature Astronomy 5, 1103

rows.name: Cloud tops
rows.label: 60,268 by 54,364 km
rows.fact: Spin flattens Saturn by a tenth: the most squashed planet of all.
rows.source: NASA Saturn Fact Sheet (NSSDCA)

rows.name: D ring
rows.label: 66,900 km
rows.fact: The faint innermost ring, reaching down toward the cloud tops.
rows.source: NASA Saturnian Rings Fact Sheet (NSSDCA)

rows.name: C ring
rows.label: 74,658 km
rows.fact: A dim, see-through ring about 5 m thick.
rows.source: NASA Saturnian Rings Fact Sheet (NSSDCA)

rows.name: B ring
rows.label: 91,975 km
rows.fact: The brightest and heaviest ring.
rows.source: NASA Saturnian Rings Fact Sheet (NSSDCA)

rows.name: Cassini Division
rows.label: about 4,700 km wide
rows.fact: A dark gap about 4,700 km wide between the two bright rings.
rows.source: NASA Saturnian Rings Fact Sheet (NSSDCA); NASA Science: Saturn facts

rows.name: A ring
rows.label: to 136,780 km
rows.fact: The main rings are 273,600 km from edge to edge and about 10 m thick.
rows.source: NASA Saturnian Rings Fact Sheet (NSSDCA); NASA Science: Saturn facts

rows.name: F ring
rows.label: 139,826 km
rows.fact: A narrow thread of ice just outside the main rings.
rows.source: NASA Saturnian Rings Fact Sheet (NSSDCA)

bodies.title: Betelgeuse
bodies.headline: A red supergiant near the end of its life, so swollen that it would fill the inner Solar System.

rows.name: Mars's orbit, for scale
rows.label: 1.5 AU
rows.fact: Put Betelgeuse where the Sun is and Mars would orbit deep inside it.
rows.source: Background.qml planetInfo (JPL elements)

rows.name: Surface
rows.label: 764 Suns wide
rows.fact: About 764 times the Sun's width: most of the way out to Jupiter.
rows.source: Joyce et al. 2020, ApJ 902, 63

bodies.title: Vega
bodies.axis: line of sight from the Sun (pole-on, about 5 degrees)
bodies.headline: A star spinning so fast it bulges. We look almost straight down on its pole.

rows.name: Flattened surface
rows.label: 2.82 by 2.36 Suns
rows.fact: One turn takes about 17 hours, so the equator bulges a fifth wider than the poles.
rows.source: Yoon et al. 2010, in van Belle 2012 review; Monnier et al. 2012 (0.71 d, pole-on); Monnier et al. 2012, ApJL 761 L3

bodies.title: Sirius
bodies.headline: The brightest star of our night sky, with a tiny dead star circling it every 50 years.

rows.name: Sirius A
rows.label: 2.06 Suns
rows.fact: A white star twice the Sun's mass, 8.6 light-years away.
rows.source: Bond et al. 2017, ApJ 840, 70

rows.name: Sirius B's orbit
rows.label: 8 to 31 AU
rows.fact: Sirius B swings between 8 and 31 AU, once every 50 years.
rows.source: Bond et al. 2017, ApJ 840, 70

rows.name: Sirius B
rows.label: Earth-sized
rows.fact: A white dwarf: the mass of the Sun pressed into a ball smaller than Earth.
rows.source: Bond et al. 2017, ApJ 840, 70

bodies.title: Alpha Centauri
bodies.headline: Our nearest neighbours: two Sun-like stars in a close dance, and a small red one far outside.

rows.name: A and B's orbit
rows.label: 11 to 36 AU
rows.fact: The pair close to Saturn's distance and part to Pluto's, once every 80 years.
rows.source: Akeson et al. 2021, AJ 162, 14; orbit range as tabulated on Wikipedia

rows.name: Proxima
rows.label: 13,000 AU
rows.fact: The nearest star to the Sun, 13,000 AU from the pair on a 550,000-year orbit.
rows.source: Kervella et al. 2017, A&A 598 L7

bodies.title: Polaris
bodies.headline: The North Star is a breathing giant: it swells and shrinks every four days.

rows.name: The Sun, for scale
rows.label: 1 Sun
rows.fact: Our Sun, drawn to the same scale.
rows.source: NASA Sun Fact Sheet (NSSDCA)

rows.name: Surface
rows.label: 46 Suns wide
rows.fact: 46 times the Sun's width and five times its mass, with a faint companion on a 30-year orbit.
rows.source: Evans et al. 2024, ApJ 971, 190; CHARA Array release on Polaris, 2024

bodies.title: Pleiades
bodies.headline: A young family of blue stars, passing through a dust cloud that glows in their light.

rows.name: Edge of the cluster
rows.label: 11.6 pc
rows.fact: Inside this line the cluster's own gravity holds about 1,250 stars together.
rows.source: Lodieu et al. 2019, A&A 628 A66

rows.name: Merope's cloud
rows.label: reflected light
rows.fact: The blue haze is a passing cloud of dust, lit by the stars and drifting toward Merope.
rows.source: NASA Hubble Messier catalog: M45

bodies.title: Hyades
bodies.headline: The nearest star cluster, slowly coming apart: stars trail 170 pc ahead of it along its orbit.

rows.name: Core
rows.label: 3.1 pc
rows.fact: The crowded middle of the cluster.
rows.source: Roeser et al. 2011, A&A 531 A92

rows.name: Edge of the cluster
rows.label: 9 pc
rows.fact: Inside this line gravity holds about 360 star systems. Those outside drift away.
rows.source: Roeser et al. 2011, A&A 531 A92; Roeser et al. 2019, A&A 621 L2

bodies.title: Omega Centauri
bodies.headline: Four million Suns in one ball of stars: probably the bare heart of a galaxy the Milky Way swallowed.

rows.name: Central black hole
rows.label: 8,200 Suns or more
rows.fact: Seven stars race round the centre: a black hole of at least 8,200 Suns holds them.
rows.source: Haeberle et al. 2024, Nature 631, 285

rows.name: Half the stars
rows.label: 10.4 pc
rows.fact: Half of the cluster's 3.9 million Suns of stars lie inside this sphere.
rows.source: Baumgardt globular cluster database: NGC 5139

bodies.title: 47 Tucanae
bodies.headline: An ancient ball of stars, packed so tightly that dead stars are spun back to life.

rows.name: Half the stars
rows.label: 6.4 pc
rows.fact: Half of the cluster's 850,000 Suns of stars lie inside this sphere.
rows.source: Baumgardt globular cluster database: NGC 104

rows.name: Pulsar swarm
rows.label: 42 pulsars
rows.fact: 42 pulsars are known near the centre, each spinning hundreds of times a second.
rows.source: Freire: the 47 Tucanae pulsars (42 known, May 2026)

bodies.title: Westerlund 1
bodies.headline: The Milky Way's heavyweight young cluster: 50,000 to 100,000 Suns of new stars.

rows.name: Magnetar
rows.label: dead star
rows.fact: A magnetar: the collapsed core of a star that has already exploded here.
rows.source: EWOCS-III (JWST), arXiv:2411.13051

rows.name: Giant stars
rows.label: 24 Wolf-Rayet stars
rows.fact: 24 Wolf-Rayet stars and over 100 blue supergiants crowd the cluster.
rows.source: EWOCS-III (JWST), arXiv:2411.13051

bodies.title: Orion Nebula
bodies.headline: A glowing hollow on the near face of a dark cloud, lit by four young stars at its heart.

rows.name: Trapezium
rows.label: 44 Suns
rows.fact: Four young stars light the whole nebula. The brightest pair weighs 44 Suns.
rows.source: Kraus et al. 2009, A&A 497, 195; NASA Hubble Messier catalog: M42

rows.name: Orion Bar
rows.label: 0.24 pc
rows.fact: The bright wall of the hollow, where starlight is eating into the cloud.
rows.source: PDRs4All III, arXiv:2310.08720 (Bar 2 arcmin from theta1 Ori C; 414 pc)
rows.derived: 2 arcmin at 414 pc (1 arcsec = 0.002 pc) = 0.24 pc, projected

rows.name: Cold cloud behind
rows.label: hidden stars
rows.fact: Behind the glow lies a cold, dark cloud where more stars are forming now.
rows.source: O'Dell 2001, ARA&A 39, 99 (not web-checked in this pass)

bodies.title: Carina Nebula · Eta Carinae
bodies.headline: A vast star nursery ruled by Eta Carinae, a double star that nearly destroyed itself in the 1840s.

rows.name: Eta Carinae
rows.label: 5 million Suns bright
rows.fact: Two giant stars circling every 5.5 years, shining like 5 million Suns.
rows.source: Smith 2017, MNRAS 471, 4465; Astronomy magazine on Eta Carinae

rows.name: Homunculus
rows.label: about 1 light-year
rows.fact: Two lobes of dust thrown out in the 1840s outburst, now a light-year long.
rows.source: NASA SVS 11568: Eta Carinae and the Homunculus

rows.name: Trumpler 14
rows.label: 2.5 million years old
rows.fact: A cluster of newborn giants whose light carves the pillars around it.
rows.source: NASA Hubble: The Carina Nebula, star birth in the extreme

bodies.title: Eagle Nebula
bodies.headline: A star nursery whose new cluster is carving the cloud into towers of gas.

rows.name: Pillars of Creation
rows.label: 4 to 5 light-years tall
rows.fact: Towers of cold gas 4 to 5 light-years tall, with stars forming at their tips.
rows.source: NASA Hubble Messier catalog: M16

rows.name: Cluster NGC 6611
rows.label: 1 to 2 million years old
rows.fact: These young stars made the pillars: their light wears the cloud away.
rows.source: NASA Hubble Messier catalog: M16

bodies.title: Lagoon Nebula
bodies.headline: A wide star nursery with a furious young star at its bright centre.

rows.name: Herschel 36
rows.label: 200,000 Suns bright
rows.fact: A star 32 times the Sun's mass and 200,000 times as bright, sculpting the cloud.
rows.source: NASA/ESA Hubble 28th anniversary: Lagoon Nebula

rows.name: Cluster NGC 6530
rows.label: several thousand stars
rows.fact: A cluster of several thousand young stars born from this cloud.
rows.source: NASA Hubble Messier catalog: M8

bodies.title: Crab Nebula
bodies.headline: The wreck of a star seen to explode in 1054, still driven by the spinning core it left behind.

rows.name: Pulsar
rows.label: 30 turns a second
rows.fact: The star's crushed core, spinning 30 times a second and powering the whole glow.
rows.source: NASA Hubble Messier catalog: M1

rows.name: Shock ring
rows.label: 1 light-year across
rows.fact: Here the pulsar's wind slams into the nebula: a ring a light-year across.
rows.source: Chandra X-ray Center: Crab Nebula (Weisskopf et al. 2000)
rows.derived: 1 ly diameter = 0.15 pc radius; the ring is tilted, its axis must be fitted on the photo

rows.name: Expanding shell
rows.label: 11 light-years
rows.fact: The star's outer layers, now 11 light-years wide and still spreading.
rows.source: NASA Hubble: a giant mosaic of the Crab Nebula
rows.derived: 11 ly = 3.4 pc across (matches the hotspot size 3.4)

bodies.title: Cygnus X / Cygnus OB2
bodies.headline: One of the Galaxy's richest star nurseries, hidden behind dust and full of heavy young stars.

rows.name: Cygnus OB2
rows.label: 16,500 Suns
rows.fact: 169 massive stars, weighing 16,500 Suns with their smaller siblings.
rows.source: Wright et al. 2015, MNRAS 449, 741

rows.name: Cosmic-ray cocoon
rows.label: 50 pc wide
rows.fact: The giant stars' winds have blown a bubble 50 pc wide, glowing in gamma rays.
rows.source: Ackermann et al. 2011, Science 334, 1103

bodies.title: Rosette Nebula
bodies.headline: A rose of glowing gas with a hole in the middle, cleared by the stars born there.

rows.name: Cluster NGC 2244
rows.label: over 70 giant stars
rows.fact: The young stars at the centre. Their winds and light hollowed out the rose.
rows.source: Rosette stellar-wind model paper, arXiv:1802.04828 (cavity radius 6.2 pc)

rows.name: Central hollow
rows.label: 6.2 pc
rows.fact: A hollow 6 pc in radius, swept clear by the cluster's winds.
rows.source: Rosette stellar-wind model paper, arXiv:1802.04828 (cavity radius 6.2 pc)

bodies.title: Ring Nebula
bodies.headline: The last breath of a Sun-like star: a glowing shell around the hot core it left bare.

rows.name: Central star
rows.label: 135,000 K
rows.fact: The star's bare core, on its way to becoming a white dwarf, lights the shell.
rows.source: Wesson et al. 2024, MNRAS 528, 3392 (JWST)

rows.name: Shell of globules
rows.label: 20,000 globules
rows.fact: The ring is broken into some 20,000 dense clumps of gas.
rows.source: Wesson et al. 2024, MNRAS 528, 3392 (JWST)

bodies.title: Helix Nebula
bodies.headline: A dying star's shell seen end-on, close enough to show thousands of comet-shaped knots.

rows.name: Central star
rows.label: over 100,000 K
rows.fact: A white dwarf in the making, hotter than 100,000 K, lights the gas it threw off.
rows.source: Helix central star, about 104,000 to 120,000 K (Napiwotzki 1999, as cited)

rows.name: Main ring
rows.label: nearly 3 light-years
rows.fact: A ring nearly 3 light-years across, studded with comet-shaped knots that point back at the star.
rows.source: NASA Hubble: iridescent glory of the nearby Helix Nebula; Matsuura et al. 2009, ApJ 700, 1067

bodies.title: Gum Nebula
bodies.headline: A faint glowing shell so wide and near that it covers 36 degrees of our southern sky.

rows.name: Shell
rows.label: about 290 pc wide
rows.fact: A huge thin shell kept glowing by two brilliant stars, Zeta Puppis and Gamma Velorum.
rows.source: Gum Nebula studies 2026 (ionised by gamma2 Vel and zeta Pup; Vela pulsar inside the shell); Background.qml hotspots (size and position)

rows.name: Vela pulsar
rows.label: dead star
rows.fact: The Vela pulsar and the wreck of its star lie inside the shell.
rows.source: Gum Nebula studies 2026 (ionised by gamma2 Vel and zeta Pup; Vela pulsar inside the shell)

bodies.headlineSource: Gum Nebula studies 2026 (ionised by gamma2 Vel and zeta Pup; Vela pulsar inside the shell)

bodies.title: Milky Way
bodies.headline: Our galaxy: a bar of old stars, a disc of spiral arms, giant bubbles above and below, and a dark halo holding it all.

rows.name: Central molecular zone
rows.label: 300 pc
rows.fact: The Galaxy's densest gas clouds crowd the inner 300 pc around the black hole.
rows.source: Henshaw et al. 2023, Protostars and Planets VII

rows.name: Bar
rows.label: 5 kpc each way
rows.fact: A bar of stars reaching 5 kpc each way, turned about 30 degrees from our line of sight.
rows.source: Wegg, Gerhard & Portail 2015, MNRAS 450, 4050

rows.name: Local Bubble
rows.label: 1,000 light-years
rows.fact: The Sun sits in a hollow 1,000 light-years wide, blown by exploding stars 14 million years ago.
rows.source: Zucker et al. 2022, Nature 601, 334 (CfA release)

rows.name: Sun's orbit
rows.label: 8.15 kpc
rows.fact: The Sun circles the centre at about 250 km a second: one lap in 200 million years.
rows.source: Bland-Hawthorn & Gerhard 2016, ARA&A 54, 529; Background.qml hotspots (size and position)
rows.derived: BH&G 2016: 248 +/- 3 km/s, 30.24 km/s/kpc, so 2 pi / Omega = 203 Myr; code 248.9 km/s at 8.15 kpc = 201 Myr

rows.name: Fermi bubbles
rows.label: about 10 kpc tall
rows.fact: Two lobes of gamma-ray light, each reaching farther than the Sun is from the centre.
rows.source: Su, Slatyer & Finkbeiner 2010, ApJ 724, 1044
rows.derived: 50 degrees and 40 degrees wide at the code's R0 8.15 kpc: tan(50)*8.15 = 9.7 kpc, 2*tan(20)*8.15 = 5.9 kpc; Su et al. quote roughly 10 kpc at R0 8.5

rows.name: eROSITA bubbles
rows.label: 14 kpc tall
rows.fact: Larger bubbles of hot gas, seen in X-rays, wrap the gamma-ray ones.
rows.source: Predehl et al. 2020, Nature 588, 227
rows.note: width not verified; take it from the eROSITA map when drawn

rows.name: Dark halo
rows.label: about 280 kpc
rows.fact: Unseen matter reaches far beyond the stars and outweighs them many times over.
rows.source: Bland-Hawthorn & Gerhard 2016, ARA&A 54, 529; Deason et al. 2020, MNRAS 496, 3929

bodies.title: Andromeda Galaxy
bodies.headline: Our great neighbour: a spiral larger than ours, falling toward us at 109 km a second.

rows.name: Central black hole
rows.label: 140 million Suns
rows.fact: A black hole of 140 million Suns: over thirty times the mass of ours.
rows.source: Bender et al. 2005, ApJ 631, 280; van der Marel et al. 2012, ApJ 753, 8

rows.name: Ring of fire
rows.label: 10 kpc
rows.fact: Most of Andromeda's new stars form in this ring, 10 kpc from the centre.
rows.source: Gordon et al. 2006, ApJL 638 L87

rows.name: Halo
rows.label: about 300 kpc
rows.fact: Thin gas and scattered stars reach about 300 kpc: almost halfway to us.
rows.source: Lehner et al. 2020, ApJ 900, 9 (Project AMIGA); Ibata et al. 2014, ApJ 780, 128 (PAndAS)

bodies.headlineSource: van der Marel et al. 2012, ApJ 753, 8

bodies.title: Triangulum Galaxy
bodies.headline: A smaller spiral with open arms, a giant star nursery, and no great black hole at its heart.

rows.name: Centre
rows.label: no giant black hole
rows.fact: No giant black hole here: anything at the centre weighs under 1,500 Suns.
rows.source: Gebhardt et al. 2001, AJ 122, 2469

rows.name: NGC 604
rows.label: 1,300 light-years
rows.fact: A star nursery 1,300 light-years across, holding over 200 of the hottest kind of star.
rows.source: NASA/JPL: peering into the tendrils of NGC 604 with Webb

rows.name: M33 X-7
rows.label: black hole, 16 Suns
rows.fact: A black hole of 16 Suns that is eclipsed by its giant partner every 3.45 days.
rows.source: Orosz et al. 2007, Nature 449, 872

bodies.title: Large Magellanic Cloud
bodies.headline: The Milky Way's biggest companion: a small galaxy of 140 billion Suns with the Local Group's fiercest star nursery.

rows.name: Tarantula Nebula
rows.label: 1,000 light-years
rows.fact: A star nursery about 1,000 light-years wide. Its heaviest stars weigh 150 to 200 Suns.
rows.source: Kalari et al. 2022, ApJ 935, 162; NASA APOD 2024 March 8: the Tarantula zone (more than 1,000 light-years)
rows.note: size from a NASA-hosted summary (about 1,000 ly); estimates run from 650 to 1,860 ly

rows.name: Supernova 1987A
rows.label: exploded 1987
rows.fact: A star seen to explode in 1987, now ringed by a glowing loop 1.4 light-years wide.
rows.source: NASA Hubble: Supernova 1987A ring (1.37 light-years)

rows.name: Magellanic Bridge
rows.label: 24 kpc
rows.fact: A bridge of gas and young stars joins the two Clouds, pulled out when they last passed.
rows.source: Magellanic Bridge: gas and young stars stripped from the SMC about 200 Myr ago (search summary; arXiv:1112.6191); Background.qml hotspots (size and position)
rows.derived: distance between the code's LMC and SMC positions = 23.8 kpc

bodies.title: Small Magellanic Cloud
bodies.headline: A small galaxy stretched by its neighbours: in places it is 23 kpc deep along our line of sight.

rows.name: Depth
rows.label: up to 23 kpc deep
rows.fact: Seen from the side this galaxy is a long cloud, up to 23 kpc deep.
rows.source: SMC red clump depth study, arXiv:1310.4824 (search summary)

rows.name: Magellanic Bridge
rows.label: 24 kpc
rows.fact: A bridge of gas and young stars joins the two Clouds, pulled out when they last passed.
rows.source: Magellanic Bridge: gas and young stars stripped from the SMC about 200 Myr ago (search summary; arXiv:1112.6191); Background.qml hotspots (size and position)
rows.derived: distance between the code's LMC and SMC positions = 23.8 kpc

rows.name: Magellanic Stream
rows.label: 200 degrees of sky
rows.fact: Gas torn from the Clouds trails across 200 degrees of our sky.
rows.source: Nidever et al. 2010, ApJ 723, 1618

bodies.headlineSource: SMC red clump depth study, arXiv:1310.4824 (search summary)

bodies.title: Sagittarius Dwarf
bodies.headline: A small galaxy the Milky Way is absorbing now, drawn out into a long stream of stars.

rows.name: Half its light
rows.label: 2.6 kpc
rows.fact: Half of this galaxy's light comes from inside this stretched oval.
rows.source: McConnachie 2012 via lib/dwarfs.js

bodies.title: Dwarf galaxies (lib/dwarfs.js)
bodies.headline: A small, faint galaxy held together mostly by matter we cannot see.

rows.name: Half its light
rows.fact: Half of this galaxy's light comes from inside this line.
rows.source: McConnachie 2012 via lib/dwarfs.js

rows.name: Dark matter
rows.label: 580,000 Suns
rows.fact: Segue 1: 580,000 Suns of mass inside 29 pc, almost none of it shining.
rows.source: Simon et al. 2011, ApJ 733, 46; McConnachie 2012 via lib/dwarfs.js

bodies.title: Local Group
bodies.headline: Two great galaxies and their small companions, bound together while the rest of the universe expands away.

rows.name: Milky Way's halo
rows.label: about 280 kpc
rows.fact: The Milky Way's dark halo: the reach of its gravity over its small companions.
rows.source: Bland-Hawthorn & Gerhard 2016, ARA&A 54, 529

rows.name: Andromeda's halo
rows.label: about 300 kpc
rows.fact: Andromeda's halo. Together the two halos span most of the 760 kpc between the galaxies.
rows.source: Lehner et al. 2020, ApJ 900, 9 (Project AMIGA); Background.qml hotspots (size and position)

rows.name: Centre of mass
rows.label: 55% of the way
rows.fact: The balance point of the group, a little over halfway to Andromeda.
rows.source: Karachentsev et al. 2009, MNRAS 393, 1265

rows.name: Edge of the group
rows.label: 0.96 Mpc
rows.fact: Inside this surface, gravity has won over cosmic expansion: 2 to 3 trillion Suns hold together.
rows.source: Karachentsev et al. 2009, MNRAS 393, 1265; van der Marel et al. 2012, ApJ 753, 8
